Name: cipher_internal_decoding_refuse
Title: Understood but Not Refused: The Decode-Then-Answer Gap in Cipher Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Encoded jailbreaks (Base64, leetspeak, ciphers) succeed not because the model fails to understand the harmful request but because decoding happens in later layers, after the refusal decision has been made on the still-encoded (benign-looking) surface form; a refusal check on the decoded internal representation closes this gap.
Related Work: Wei et al. (2023, competing objectives / mismatched generalization); Yuan et al. (2024, CipherChat); Handa et al. (2024) cipher jailbreaks. Prior work explains cipher attacks as capability-safety mismatch behaviorally. We distinguish by mechanistically locating where decoding occurs relative to where refusal is computed, testing the 'refusal-before-decode' timing hypothesis, and intervening by re-checking refusal on the post-decode representation.
Abstract: Encoding a harmful request (Base64, ciphers, leetspeak) frequently bypasses safety while the model still complies with the decoded intent, suggesting the model understands the harm but does not refuse. We hypothesize a timing mechanism: the refusal decision is computed in earlier-to-middle layers on the encoded surface form, which looks benign, whereas full decoding of the harmful meaning completes only in later layers—so refusal fires before the harmful content is internally legible. We test this by using the logit lens and probes to locate the layer where the decoded harmful meaning becomes internally represented, and compare it to the layer where the refusal direction is normally decisive, predicting decoding lags refusal for successful cipher attacks. We validate causally by intervening: add a refusal re-check that reads the refusal direction from the later, post-decode layers (or steer refusal using late-layer harmful-intent representation), and measure restored refusal on cipher/encoding attacks without harming benign encoded tasks (e.g., legitimate Base64 handling). We compare to decode-then-moderate pipelines. We predict decoding lags the refusal decision, explaining the attack, and that a late-layer refusal re-check substantially reduces encoded-jailbreak success at low cost. The contribution is a mechanistic, timing-based explanation of a major jailbreak family and a targeted late-layer intervention grounded in where meaning versus safety are computed.
Experiments: 1) Encoded harmful prompts (Base64, ROT13, leetspeak, custom cipher) vs plaintext; measure ASR. 2) Logit-lens/probes to find layer where decoded harmful meaning appears; find layer where refusal direction is decisive; compare timing. 3) Causal: late-layer refusal re-check / steer refusal from late-layer intent representation; measure encoded-jailbreak ASR and benign encoded-task performance. 4) Baseline: decode-then-Llama-Guard. Models: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Some encodings may be decoded early, weakening the timing story. Late-layer re-check adds compute. Benign encoded tasks may be over-refused. Very novel ciphers may not decode internally at all (then no harm either). Model-dependent layer structure.
